sections.title: The Era of Translational Retinal Therapeutics
sections.content: Contemporary ophthalmic literature represents a monumental transition from short-acting, single-pathway anti-VEGF agents to dual-pathway, multi-target molecular therapeutics and sustained-release depot systems. Research is heavily focused on extending treatment durability, targeting the complement cascade for dry AMD, utilizing gene-delivered biofactories, and implementing autonomous deep-learning systems to optimize patient triage and disease management.

sections.title: Dual Pathway Target: Faricimab (Vabysmo)
content: Step 1: Double Inhibition - Simultaneously binds and neutralizes both VEGF-A and Angiopoietin-2 (Ang-2).
Step 2: Vascular Stabilization - Ang-2 inhibition restores endothelial stability and decreases vascular leakage, synergizing with VEGF blockade.
Step 3: Clinical Trials validation - TENAYA/LUCERNE (nAMD) and YOSEMITE/RHINE (DME) trials demonstrated non-inferiority to Aflibercept.
Step 4: Interval Extension - Up to 60% of patients achieved Q16W dosing intervals at 1 year, maintaining visual and anatomical outcomes.

sections.title: Sustained-Release Intraocular Drug Delivery
content: Susvimo (Port Delivery System): Permanent refillable implant surgical system delivering a customized formulation of Ranibizumab 100 mg/mL. Archway trial demonstrated sustained visual acuity with refills only every 24 weeks.

Durysta (Bimatoprost SR): Biodegradable 10 mcg intracameral implant for Open-Angle Glaucoma. Phase 3 ARTEMIS trials showed a single implant maintains target IOP for up to 12 months in a subset of patients.

iDose TR (Travoprost Intraocular Implant): Non-biodegradable titanium implant anchored in the trabecular meshwork. Phase 3 trials showed sustained drug delivery and robust IOP lowering over 3 years, significantly reducing daily topical drop burdens.

sections.title: Myopia Control Interventions
content: LAMP Study Insights: Atropine 0.05% is significantly more effective than 0.01% in slowing axial elongation and spherical equivalent progression, with minimal impact on pupil size and accommodation.
Optical Defocus (DIMS / H.A.L.T. Lenses): Induces peripheral myopic defocus, keeping light rays in front of the peripheral retina to halt axial length elongation signals.
Orthokeratology: Reshapes the central cornea while creating mid-peripheral epithelial steepening, effectively creating a natural optical defocus mechanism.

sections.title: Presbyopia Pharmacotherapy
content: Pilocarpine 1.25% (Vuity): First FDA-approved miotic drop for presbyopia. Utilizes dynamic pupil modulation to achieve a pinhole effect.
Landmark GEMINI 1 & 2 Trials: Demonstrated rapid onset (15 mins) and sustained near visual acuity gains (3-line gain in photopic near DCNVA at day 30, hour 3) without compromising distance vision.
Mechanism of Action: Iris sphincter and ciliary muscle contraction. Temporary mild headache and conjunctival hyperemia are the most common transient side effects.

sections.title: Thyroid Eye Disease: Teprotumumab
content: Step 1: Target Binding - Teprotumumab is a human monoclonal antibody targeting the Insulin-like Growth Factor-1 Receptor (IGF-1R).
Step 2: Pathway Blockade - Inhibits the retro-orbital fibroblast activation pathway, reducing extracellular matrix deposition and hyaluronic acid synthesis.
Step 3: OPTIC Trial Results - Achieved clinically significant proptosis reduction (mean of >2mm reduction) and rapid improvement in diplopia grades.
Step 4: Monitoring Protocol - Baseline and post-treatment audiometry required due to risks of hearing impairment; monitor blood glucose levels closely.

sections.title: Landmark DRCR.net Diabetic Retinopathy Trials
content: Protocol T (DME Comparison): For baseline visual acuity of 20/50 or worse, Aflibercept demonstrated superior visual gains over Ranibizumab and Bevacizumab. No significant difference existed when baseline VA was 20/32 to 20/40.

Protocol W (Prevention of DME): Intravitreal Aflibercept in eyes with moderate-to-severe NPDR significantly decreased the development of vision-threatening complications (CI-DME or PDR) over 2 years, but did not show a visual acuity benefit compared to sham injection.

Protocol V (Mild DME with Good Vision): Eyes with center-involved DME and visual acuity of 20/25 or better can be managed safely with initial observation and deferred anti-VEGF therapy only if vision worsens, with no long-term visual loss difference compared to immediate anti-VEGF.

sections.title: Modern Therapeutics Safety Red Flags
content: Syfovre (Pegcetacoplan): Rare but devastating intraocular inflammation and occlusive retinal vasculitis (incidence of ~0.01% per injection); mandates strict aseptic prep and close post-injection monitoring.
Susvimo (Port Delivery System): Increased risk of endophthalmitis (3.2-fold higher than monthly injections in trials), conjunctival retraction, erosion, and exposure over the implant site.
Tepezza (Teprotumumab): Risk of permanent sensorineural hearing loss, severe muscle spasms, and exacerbation of pre-existing inflammatory bowel disease.
Vuity (Pilocarpine 1.25%): Risk of peripheral retinal tears, vitreoretinal traction, and retinal detachment, especially in highly myopic patients due to ciliary muscle spasm.

sections.title: Mnemonic for Evaluating Modern Clinical Trials

content.explanation: F - Funding & Conflicts: Be aware of industry-sponsored vs. investigator-initiated bias. A - Anatomical vs. Functional outcomes: Note the discordance between OCT improvements and actual BCVA letter gains. S - Safety Signals: Check for low-incidence but high-severity adverse events. T - Treatment Durability: Assess real-world patient retention and compliance compared to optimal clinical trial regimens.

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always perform a thorough peripheral retinal exam before prescribing presbyopia-correcting miotics to rule out pre-existing retinal tears, lattice degeneration, or high myopia-associated pathology.

When initiating complement inhibitor therapy for dry AMD, counsel patients that these injections stabilize the progressive tissue loss rate but will not restore lost photoreceptors or improve visual acuity.

For diabetic macular edema with good baseline vision, deferring anti-VEGF treatment until visual deterioration is clinically proven remains a safe, evidence-based strategy supported by DRCR.net Protocol V.
